finalArgument.thesis: Christianity is rationally warranted as the cumulative explanation of historical testimony, transformative effects, moral experience, and coherent divine character.
premises: Recoverable early testimony provides defeasible historical evidence that Jesus was regarded as divine and that followers sincerely proclaimed his resurrection.
Empty-tomb traditions, conversions, costly adherence, immediate proclamation, and rapid movement emergence jointly fit resurrection better than separately assembled natural explanations.
Christian teaching encouraged countercultural equality, forgiveness, sacrificial concern, and hope in ways expected if reality is personally and morally purposive.
Limited public manifestation can preserve voluntary relational trust while historical, experiential, and moral evidence still provides responsible inquirers sufficient grounds for commitment.
Protective divine wrath is compatible with love when it remains proportionate, opposes genuine harm, secures justice, and permits restoration through forgiveness.
finalArgument.conclusion: Because these partially independent considerations reinforce one another, Christian commitment may be rational even when no individual evidential strand establishes certainty.

newArguments.title: Comparative cumulative likelihood
newArguments.text: Knechtle could compare how expected each historical, moral, and experiential observation is under Christianity and named alternatives. He should discount dependent sources, document every premise, and give no strand more weight than its provenance permits. This would transform an enumerated cumulative case into an explicit inference, showing whether several modest considerations jointly favor resurrection and theism without pretending that any single item demonstrates a miracle.

newArguments.title: Public and private warrant
newArguments.text: The defense could separate publicly shareable history from personally accessible experience. Public evidence would establish a common floor, while conscience, transformation, or perceived encounter could rationally raise confidence for particular people when tested for reliability and defeaters. This framework uses Dillahunty’s concession about person-relative warrant while avoiding the stronger claim that private evidence obligates outsiders who cannot inspect it.

newArguments.title: Specific moral predictions
newArguments.text: Rather than inferring truth from social benefit, Knechtle could identify costly practices specifically predicted by Jesus’s teaching in its Roman setting, document their early occurrence, and compare rival influences. Surprising, distinctive fulfillment might offer limited indirect confirmation if Christianity predicts it better than alternatives. The argument should acknowledge contrary Christian conduct and avoid claiming that usefulness alone verifies supernatural doctrine.
